tts.text: A baby delivered by forceps delivery was found to have absent red reflex in left eye. What is the most likely cause? Option A. Congenital cataract. Option B. Retinal detachment. Option C. Retinoblastoma. Option D. Corneal birth trauma.

scenarioAr: مولود وُلد باستخدام forceps لديه absent red reflex بالعين اليسرى؛ المطلوب السبب.
explanationAr: المفتاح A: Congenital cataract. الأصل يحيل فقط إلى سؤال آخر رقم 188 ولا يقدم هنا تعليلًا مفصلًا يميز cataract من corneal birth trauma؛ لذلك لم يُعتبر التشخيص محسومًا لمجرد نقل المفتاح. حُفظ النص الأصلي بدل تغيير السؤال إلى سؤال عن المفتاح.
incorrectOptionsAr: B وC وD: بدائل موجودة في الأصل، لكنه لا يقدم مناقشة منفصلة لاستبعادها؛ نقص الفحص التفصيلي يقتضي المراجعة.
clinicalPearl: A source answer with only a cross-reference is not an independently established diagnosis.

tts.text: An infant was found to have strabismus and abnormal red reflex in one eye. What is your best next step? Option A. CT scan. Option B. TORCH screening.

scenarioAr: رضيع لديه strabismus وabnormal red reflex بعين واحدة؛ المطلوب best next step.
explanationAr: المصدر يقول إن B قد تكون الإجابة، لكنه يصرح بأن الأفضل urgent ophthalmology referral وقد يلزم examination under anesthesia، وهي خطوة غير موجودة في الخيارات. ويذكر تجنب CT روتينيًا للتشخيص عند احتمال retinoblastoma بسبب التعرض للإشعاع. حُفظ التعارض دون إعادة صياغة المطلوب إلى مجرد اختيار ما طُبع بالمفتاح.
incorrectOptionsAr: A: لا يفضله الشرح كفحص تشخيصي أولي عند احتمال RB1-related retinoblastoma. B: TORCH tests تُوجه حسب التاريخ والفحص ولا تستبدل التقييم العيني العاجل الذي يناقشه المصدر.

Because retinoblastoma is among the most common causes of lе սkοсоriа in children, and because of the 
grave consequences to the child's life and vision if rеti ոοblаѕtоma goes undiagnosed, urgent referral to an 
ophthalmologist specializing in rеti ոοblаѕtоma is essential for all children with lе սkοϲoriа at the time 
lеսkοсоriа is first detected.  The ophthalmologist performs a comprehensive ophthalmologic examination 
as described in the following sections. Anterior segment and dilated funduscopic examination are 
performed in the offic e along with ocular սltrаѕοոοgrарhу. Many children referred with lе սkοсоriа will 
require radiologic testing and/or examination under anesthesia (ΕUΑ) to establish a definitive diagnosis or

Use of computed tomography (CT) for diagnosis should be avoided, given the risk of radiation exposure in 
a child with a possible RB1 gene mutation. [UpToDate] 
 
Laboratory evaluation of the child with lе սkοcοriа is guided by the history and physical examination 
findings and may include: [UpToDate]

antibodies. 
• Metabolic studies (eg, for galactosemia) if the history is suggestive.  
• Genetic testing may be warranted if the history and clinical findings suggest a specific genetic 
disorder (eg, incontinentia pigmenti). Genetic testing is also warranted in the evaluation of

tts.text: A 2-year-old boy presented with crossing eyes. On examinations, strabismus was noted on cover/uncover test. Also, there is yellow / white pupillary reflex. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A. Retinoblastoma. Option B. Very high myopia.

scenarioAr: طفل عمره سنتان لديه strabismus بالفحص وyellow/white pupillary reflex؛ المطلوب التشخيص.
explanationAr: المفتاح A: Retinoblastoma. يصف المصدر leukocoria كعرض كلاسيكي، ويذكر أن strabismus قد يكون الشكوى الأولى. هذا ربط من النص التعليمي وليس إثباتًا تشخيصيًا قائمًا على فحص طفل حقيقي.
incorrectOptionsAr: B: very high myopia ليست الإجابة المختارة؛ الشرح يعتمد على white pupillary reflex مع strabismus ولا يقدم تفاصيل فحص refractive إضافية.
clinicalPearl: The source connects strabismus plus a white pupillary reflex with retinoblastoma.
sourceExplanationEn:
Retinoblastoma classically presents with leukocoria, a white pupillary reflex, which often is first noticed 
when a red reflex is not present at a routine newborn or well-child examination or in a flash photograph of 
the child. Strabismus often is an initial presenting complaint. [Nelson]

tts.text: A 16-month-old girl presented with crossing eyes. On examinations, cover/uncover test was normal with no correction, also, light was in the middle of both eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A. Pseudostrabismus. Option B. Myopia with strabismus. Option C. Accommodative esotropia.

scenarioAr: طفلة عمرها 16 شهرًا تبدو عيناها متقاطعتين لكن cover/uncover طبيعي وcorneal light reflex متناظر؛ المطلوب التشخيص.
explanationAr: المفتاح A: Pseudostrabismus. يشرح المصدر أن wide nasal bridge أوepicanthal folds قد يعطيان مظهر esotropia كاذبًا، بينما symmetric corneal reflex وnormal cover/uncover يدعمان المحاذاة الطبيعية. صورة PREP المذكورة في الشرح ليست مرفقة هنا؛ الـstem نفسه يقدم نتائج الفحص اللازمة.
incorrectOptionsAr: B وC: يتضمنان strabismus حقيقيًا، بينما النتائج المذكورة في السؤال والمناقشة تدعم محاذاة العينين الطبيعية.
clinicalPearl: Symmetric corneal light reflexes and a normal cover test support pseudostrabismus in the source.
sourceExplanationEn:
The infant in this vignette has pseudostrabismus. Although the right eye in the image appears to be turned 
in, the symmetric corneal reflex and normal cover/uncover test results rule out true strabismus. In reality, 
the epicanthal folds result in a wide na sal bridge that covers the white part of the eye creating the illusion 
of esotropia. [Question 169 in PREP 2019] 
 
Pseudoesotropia is the most common form of pseudostrabismus. It is the false appearance of eye crossing 
that most commonly occurs in infants and children with a wide nasal bridge and/or large epicanthal folds 
during the first few years of life. It is an optical illusion in which the wide nasal bridge or epicanthal folds 
cover the nasal sclera, making the eye appear esotropic, particularly when the child looks in lateral gaze. 
Normal ocular alignment is demonstr ated by symmetric corneal light reflexes and the cover and 
cover/uncover tests. [UpToDate]

sourceAnswerText: A? Similar question in PREP 2020 (question 98) answered as spasmus nutans (although congenital nystagmus was one of the choices). This question came in PART 2 2023. Noted that, PREP 2020 question has other clinical findings, not only abnormal eye rhythmic movements.

tts.text: The parent of a 4-month-old baby came with concerns about abnormal eye rhythmic movements especially when he looks to the left. Other than that, examinations were normal. MRI done and was normal. What is the most likely cause? Option A. Congenital nystagmus. Option B. Neuroblastoma.

scenarioAr: رضيع عمره 4 أشهر لديه rhythmic eye movements خاصة بالنظر لليسار مع فحص وMRI طبيعيين؛ المطلوب السبب.
explanationAr: المفتاح مطبوع A? والبديلان كلاهما موسوم A في الأصل. الشرح يقارن congenital nystagmus وspasmus nutans، ويقول إن سؤال PREP المقتبس يحوي تفاصيل إضافية غير موجودة هنا. لم تُضف torticollis أوhead titubation للـstem. استُخدم B كمفتاح تقني للبديل الثاني فقط، مع حفظ sourceKey=A وإعلان خطأ الترقيم.
incorrectOptionsAr: البديل الثاني Neuroblastoma: يناقش المصدر opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia كسياق مختلف، لكن لا يجوز حسم هذا السؤال من normal MRI وحده. غياب spasmus nutans من الخيارات والـrecall الملتبس يبقيان السؤال للمراجعة.
clinicalPearl: Preserve both the uncertain diagnosis and the duplicate option label in the source audit.
sourceExplanationEn:
Two types of nystagmus are described: jerk nystagmus and pendular nystagmus. Jerk nystagmus is 
described as a slow drift of the eye in one direction with a quick corrective “jerk” in the opposite direction. 
It is further characterized by direction and appearance (downbeat, upbeat, horizontal, torsional, or mixed). 
Pendular nystagmus is a slow sinusoidal oscillation without accompanying fast phase. Jerk nystagmus is 
more common than pendular nystagmus and results from imbalances in the vestibular inputs. [PREP 2020, 
Question 98] 
 
Congenital or infantile nystagmus presents in the first 6 months after birth and is characterize by a conjugate 
horizontal oscillation with a mixture of jerk and pendular features. Although present at birth, it is often first 
appreciated and diagnosed around 3 months of age as infants begin to fixate on objects. The main 
differential diagnosis is spasmus nutans. The 2 conditions can be distinguished by age of onset, appearance 
of nystagmus, and accompanying features. [PREP 2020, Question 98] 
 
The infant in this vignette (question 98 in PREP 2020) has nystagmus, torticollis, and head titubation, a 
triad of clinical findings consistent with spasmus nutans. A rare condition, spasmus nutans typically 
presents in the first year, usually after 6 months of age, and resolves during childhood. All 3 compone nts 
are not required for the diagnosis. Head titubation and torticollis can occur intermittently and may be a 
compensatory movement for the nystagmus, resulting in the appearance of “spasm.” The nystag mus in 
spasmus nutans is a pendular nystagmus characterized by small, fast, usually horizontal oscillations that 
can be unilateral or bilateral and is dysconjugate. [PREP 2020, Question 98] 
 
Distinct from nystagmus, opsoclonus -myoclonus-ataxia syndrome is an autoimmune, sometimes 
paraneoplastic syndrome, characterized by chaotic irregular “dancing eye” movements, intermittent 
myoclonic jerks, and ataxia of the body. Classically associated with neuroblastoma, opsoclonus -
myoclonus-ataxia syndrome can also occur as a post -viral autoimmune condition. [PREP 2020, Question 
98]
